title: The Tail Matters
briefing: As a Senior Risk Analyst you now run the quantitative work. Hollis Varga is setting next year's budget provision for stock spoilage and asks for one number.
You have the spoilage loss history and the Monte Carlo tool at your workstation. Hollis's instinct is to budget the average.

context.text: Hollis liked your Harrowgate flood work: "You told me what we actually keep. Do the same here."
The Eastfield breakdown is in this year's loss history, which makes the year look worse than usual.

evidence.title: Spoilage events, last 5 years
body: About 6 events a year (Poisson-like). Single-event losses: median 18,000; 90th percentile 95,000; largest 410,000.

evidence.title: Monte Carlo run (10,000 trials, seed 7) prepared by the team
Finance budgeting note
evidence.body: Provisions are set so the business is not surprised more than one year in ten. Any overspend above budget must be found from cuts elsewhere in the same year.

questions.prompt: Given the policy ('not surprised more than one year in ten'), which figure should set the provision?

options.label: P90: 268,000
options.feedback: One year in ten above the provision is exactly the 90th percentile.

options.label: The mean: 152,000
options.feedback: Budgeting the mean means overspending in roughly four years out of ten for a skewed loss like this.

options.label: The median: 121,000
options.feedback: Half of all years would overspend.

options.label: 402,000: the worst year in the history, so the provision has always been enough
options.feedback: Ties up money against a rarer outcome than the policy requires.

questions.prompt: Why is the mean (152,000) above the median (121,000)?

options.label: A few large events pull the average up: losses are right-skewed
options.feedback: Severity has a long right tail (largest 410,000 against a median of 18,000).

options.label: Too few trials: with more simulations the mean and median would converge
options.feedback: Mean above median is expected for skewed loss distributions.

options.label: Inflation: later years have larger losses, which lifts the average above the middle year
options.feedback: Inflation would shift both, not separate them.

questions.prompt: How do you present the result to Hollis?

options.label: "Budget 268,000. A typical year costs 120,000-150,000; one in twenty could exceed 340,000."
options.feedback: A number to act on, plus the range and tail in plain words.

options.label: "The simulation's expected annual loss is 152,000: that is the best single estimate to budget."
options.feedback: One number hides the risk he asked you to manage.

options.label: The histogram and percentile table, with a note on how to read each percentile

questions.prompt: Hollis asks how to protect against the 1-in-100 year (about 560,000). Your authority is 75,000.

options.label: Get a quote for stock cover above 300,000 a year and compare the premium with the loss it removes
options.feedback: Transfer the tail and keep the frequent small losses: the classic split. You test the price before committing.

options.label: Raise the provision to 560,000 so that even a 1-in-100 year is covered from the budget
Accept the tail: a 1-in-100 year is too remote to plan the budget around
options.feedback: Rare is not never. A year like that would force deep cuts mid-year.

questions.prompt: Operations dispute the model: "Last year was a one-off." How do you respond?

options.label: Walk them through the inputs, show the result with and without last year, and ask for better data
options.feedback: Transparent assumptions build trust; testing the disputed year answers the challenge directly.

options.label: Explain that the model follows the agreed methodology, so its inputs are not open to negotiation
options.feedback: Pulling rank wins the meeting and loses the relationship.

options.label: Exclude last year as an outlier, since Operations know the cause and it is unlikely to recur
options.feedback: Dropping inconvenient data biases the result.

lesson: For skewed losses, the average is not a budget. Pick the percentile the policy asks for, and explain the range and the tail in plain words.
